column1: # Judged relevance cases. A case PASSES when at least one of the top-k display names matches an
# acceptable pattern AND none of them match an unacceptable one. Both columns matter:
# with only an acceptable pattern, a case passes on any list holding one good row however much
#   Acceptable = "a person who typed this would call this result correct." Unacceptable = "seeing
#   this in the top five is a bug", which in practice means a derivative or a composite dish
#   crowding out the plain food: juice/flour/powder for a fruit or grain, soup/pie/cake for an
#   ingredient, a dish that merely *contains* the thing.
#   Cases were written from what a correct answer looks like, NOT from what the ranking currently
#   returns. Some cases fail on purpose. Do not weaken one to make it pass.
#   Where a national table lacks the plain food -- Swedish has no bare "Banan", only
#   Bananchips/Banan torkad/Banan friterad -- the acceptable pattern also admits the plain row
#   another source supplies, because reaching it is exactly what the fallback shelf is for.
# WRITE (?i) ON EVERY ALTERNATIVE. The cell is split on `|` before compiling. The evaluator now
# reads the flag once for the whole cell, but writing it per alternative stays the clearer habit.
# ------------------------------------------------- Small-table misses: the fallback shelf's job
# bedca (736 rows) has no oats and no lentils of its own; swiss has neither those nor cucumber.
# A reader in Spain or Switzerland must still reach them, from another generic source rather than
# Nordic and German tables store the basic food as a compound -- Vollkornbrot, Skummetmælk,
# Ruisleipä, Sødmælk -- while FTS5 prefix matching only reaches token prefixes. A reader typing
# the bare word therefore cannot reach the compound, and a reader typing the compound cannot
# reach a table that separates it ("Svin, nakkekoteletter"). These cases pin both directions.
# They are expected to fail until that is addressed; see the findings.
